notable_similarities: Every device presents multiple conflicting service identities simultaneously on different ports — e.g., the same IP serves FortiManager, ASUS AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Confluence, and ComfyUI concurrently, which is physically impossible for a single real device

MQTT (1883/8883), Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL appear across multiple devices alongside HTTP services, consistent with IoT honeypot infrastructure designed to attract diverse scanner/attacker profiles

Hardware fingerprints (FortiSwitch, ASUS RT-AX68U, EasyIO 30P, Gaugetech) repeat identically across geographically dispersed IPs, which would be statistically improbable for organic device deployments
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 consists of 3532 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally, each simulating a large number of heterogeneous IoT, OT, network, and enterprise services simultaneously on dozens of non-standard ports — a pattern strongly indicative of honeypot or deception infrastructure. The devices share a common fingerprint template featuring recurring application titles, hardware identifiers, and TLS certificate patterns that are internally inconsistent and mismatched to their AWS hosting context. The cluster is unified by its AWS-only hosting, extreme port/service density per IP, synthetic certificate diversity, and the systematic co-presence of IoT, ICS/SCADA, VPN, and enterprise application fingerprints that no single physical device could legitimately host.

common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.
common_patterns.hardware: HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U are the most frequently fingerprinted hardware across devices, often co-occurring on the same IP. Fortinet FortiSwitch hardware also recurs. These are likely honeypot or emulated device signatures.
common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. Mix of HTTP, Unknown Protocol (TLS-wrapped), DNS, MQTT, SMB, IPP, SSH, SSDP/UPnP, and PostgreSQL services. No device is limited to a single service role.

FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate login pages, GlobalProtect Portal, ASUS Login, CyberPanel, PaperCut, Ray Dashboard, Mirth Connect, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver pages also recur across multiple IPs.
common_patterns.certificates: TLS certificates are highly diverse and inconsistent per port — mixing legitimate CA-signed certs (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust, Amazon) with self-signed device certs (Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, Siemens, HP, MikroTik, Honeywell, ICS/SCADA vendors). Certificate subjects frequently reference ICS/OT systems (SCADA, PLC, IEC61850, DNP3, Honeywell Experion, Yokogawa CENTUM, Siemens SIMATIC WinCC), healthcare (EMR, DICOM, Epic, Allscripts, DirectTrust), and enterprise IT (Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Splunk, HashiCorp Vault).
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS consistently resolves to AWS EC2 regional hostnames (ap-southeast-7, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, af-south-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1, ap-southeast-3). Two devices (54.85.68.8, 18.216.147.127) have no reverse DNS.

distribution_characteristics.organizational: All devices are AWS EC2 instances across Amazon's regional data center subsidiaries. No non-Amazon ASNs present. The cluster represents a globally distributed set of AWS-hosted endpoints, not on-premises IoT devices.

notable_similarities: Identical Confluence login page HTML with the same hardcoded atlassian-token, build number (8703), and base-url placeholder across all devices and ports — strongly indicating a shared template or honeypot deployment rather than real Confluence instances.

Every device presents an implausibly broad and heterogeneous service portfolio (20–55+ ports) combining enterprise IT, networking, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT fingerprints simultaneously — characteristic of high-interaction honeypots or IoT emulation platforms.

HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.

common_patterns.dns: Mix of ISP-assigned dynamic reverse DNS and custom *.synology.me DDNS hostnames

distribution_characteristics.geographic_spread: Globally distributed across Europe (NL, DE, CH, FR, PL), Asia-Pacific (CN, HK), and North America (CA) — consistent with consumer/prosumer self-hosted deployments worldwide
distribution_characteristics.asn_types: Predominantly residential and SMB ISPs (Deutsche Telekom, Swisscom, Ziggo, SFR, Netia, HKBN, ChinaNet) rather than datacenter ASNs, confirming home/small-office deployments
distribution_characteristics.no_geographic_concentration: No single country or ASN dominates; distribution reflects Synology's global consumer market share

notable_similarities: All devices expose Synology DSM web interface on port 5000/5001 with identical HTML structure, favicon paths, and msapplication metadata — the strongest clustering signal
Synology self-signed CA certificate (C=TW, L=Taipei, O=Synology Inc.) on port 5001 is a near-universal fingerprint across the cluster
Favicon versioning pattern (?v=40438 or ?v=4398) in webman paths distinguishes DSM version generations within the cluster
WS-Discovery on port 3702 and unknown protocols on 3261-3265 are Synology-specific service discovery mechanisms appearing consistently
Many devices layer smart home automation (Home Assistant, ioBroker, Node-RED, MQTT, Grafana) on top of the Synology NAS — indicating a 'home server hub' usage pattern
nginx as the reverse proxy frontend is universal, reflecting Synology DSM's internal architecture
Let's Encrypt certificates using *.synology.me DDNS subdomains confirm use of Synology's free DDNS service for remote access
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: Predominantly AS58224 (TCI - Telecommunication Company of Iran / Iran Information Technology Company PJSC), with a few devices on smaller Iranian ISPs (AS43754 ASIATECH, AS42337 RESPINA, AS31549 RASANA, AS204650 ERTEBATATESTABLEAVARVAND). All devices are country_code: IR.
common_patterns.os: Where detected, Microsoft Windows Server 2012 R2 is the only identified OS. Most devices have no OS fingerprint.
common_patterns.software: Near-universal use of Microsoft IIS (predominantly version 10.0) and ASP.NET across all HTTP services. jQuery (versions 2.1.0, 2.1.4, 3.6.0) and Twitter Bootstrap appear frequently as frontend libraries. Swagger UI appears on one device.
common_patterns.hardware: DICOM-104 (medical imaging protocol) is present on the vast majority of devices, making it the single strongest hardware/protocol commonality. DVR_IP ports appear on a subset of devices. IKE-500 (VPN) appears on a few.
common_patterns.services: DICOM-104 is the near-universal service. HTTP on various non-standard ports is common. MDNS-5353 (mDNS/Bonjour) appears on many devices. MIKROTIK_BW-2000 appears on several, indicating MikroTik network equipment. VPN-related services (IKE-500, L2TP-1701, PPTP-1723) appear on a subset. MSSQL-1433 (SQL Server 15.0.2000) appears on at least two devices.
common_patterns.http_tags_and_favicons: The most dominant HTTP application fingerprint is 'Marco Pacs' — a PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) — appearing across many devices on various ports (80, 443, 6527, 6528, 1360, etc.). Other medical software titles include 'OHIF Viewer' (DICOM web viewer), 'MedPacs', 'PayvastERP', and Persian-language medical/laboratory portals (online lab results, radiology results, hospital reporting panels). Titles are predominantly in Persian (Farsi).
common_patterns.certificates: Multiple devices share wildcard certificate CN=*.marcopacs.net issued by Certum (Unizeto Technologies S.A. / Asseco Data Systems S.A., Poland), confirming a shared Marco PACS deployment. One device has CN=pacsoxin.com from the same Certum CA.
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS is largely absent. One device resolves to shatel.ir (an Iranian ISP).

distribution_characteristics.geographic: All 44 devices are located in Iran (IR). No cross-country distribution.
distribution_characteristics.organizational: Majority are under TCI (Telecommunication Company of Iran) and its subsidiary Iran Information Technology Company PJSC — the dominant national telecom. A minority are on smaller Iranian commercial ISPs (Asiatech, Respina, Shatel, Ertebat Sabet). This suggests these are customer-premise deployments (hospitals/clinics) connected via various Iranian ISPs, not a single data center.
distribution_characteristics.network_blocks: Devices span multiple /21 to /24 BGP prefixes, consistent with geographically distributed end-customer sites rather than a co-located deployment.

notable_similarities: DICOM-104 open port is the strongest clustering signal — present on nearly all devices, identifying them as medical imaging systems (PACS servers).
Marco PACS application (title 'Marco Pacs', wildcard cert *.marcopacs.net) is deployed across a large subset, indicating a single Iranian medical imaging software vendor's customer base.
Uniform Microsoft IIS 10.0 + ASP.NET stack across all HTTP-serving devices points to a standardized deployment template.
MDNS-5353 exposure on many devices suggests local-network service discovery is inadvertently exposed to the internet, a common misconfiguration in clinical environments.
MikroTik presence (MIKROTIK_BW-2000, RouterOS HTTP title) on several devices indicates MikroTik routers are used as the network gateway at these sites, with management interfaces exposed.
Persian-language web UIs (lab results, radiology, hospital HIS portals) confirm these are Iranian healthcare facility deployments.
Shared Certum CA (Polish CA) for *.marcopacs.net certificates across multiple IPs confirms a single vendor (Marco PACS) managing TLS certificates for its customer installations.
DVR_IP ports on a subset suggest co-located IP camera/DVR systems at the same facilities, broadening the attack surface.
report.cluster_summary: This cluster represents Iranian healthcare facility servers — primarily hospitals and diagnostic imaging centers — running the Marco PACS medical imaging platform (and related HIS/lab software) on a standardized Microsoft IIS/ASP.NET stack. The near-universal presence of open DICOM-104 ports, shared *.marcopacs.net wildcard certificates, and Persian-language medical web portals confirm these are deployments of a single Iranian medical software vendor across distributed clinical sites. Security concerns include exposed DICOM, mDNS, MikroTik management interfaces, DVR ports, and in some cases open MSSQL and SMB services directly on the internet.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: All devices belong to AS16509 (AMAZON-02) or AS14618 (AMAZON-AES), both operated by Amazon.com, Inc. — 100% AWS-hosted infrastructure.

common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.
common_patterns.hardware: HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U are the most frequently fingerprinted hardware across devices, often co-occurring on the same IP. Fortinet FortiSwitch hardware also recurs. These are likely honeypot or emulated device signatures.
common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. Mix of HTTP, Unknown Protocol (TLS-wrapped), DNS, MQTT, SMB, IPP, SSH, SSDP/UPnP, and PostgreSQL services. No device is limited to a single service role.
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Confluence login page HTML (identical atlassian-token 'e68dfa45d0ec9701eac9e51568b6020923c96741', build number 8703, base-url 'https://www.example.com') is replicated verbatim across all devices and ports. FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate login pages, GlobalProtect Portal, ASUS Login, CyberPanel, PaperCut, Ray Dashboard, Mirth Connect, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver pages also recur across multiple IPs.
common_patterns.certificates: TLS certificates are highly diverse and inconsistent per port — mixing legitimate CA-signed certs (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust, Amazon) with self-signed device certs (Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, Siemens, HP, MikroTik, Honeywell, ICS/SCADA vendors). Certificate subjects frequently reference ICS/OT systems (SCADA, PLC, IEC61850, DNP3, Honeywell Experion, Yokogawa CENTUM, Siemens SIMATIC WinCC), healthcare (EMR, DICOM, Epic, Allscripts, DirectTrust), and enterprise IT (Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Splunk, HashiCorp Vault).
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS consistently resolves to AWS EC2 regional hostnames (ap-southeast-7, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, af-south-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1, ap-southeast-3). Two devices (54.85.68.8, 18.216.147.127) have no reverse DNS.

distribution_characteristics.geographic: Global AWS footprint spanning at least 8 regions: AP Southeast (Bangkok), EU Central (Frankfurt), EU West (Paris), AF South (Cape Town), AP Northeast (Osaka), ME Central (UAE), AP Southeast (Jakarta), US East (Ohio/Virginia).
distribution_characteristics.organizational: All devices are AWS EC2 instances across Amazon's regional data center subsidiaries. No non-Amazon ASNs present. The cluster represents a globally distributed set of AWS-hosted endpoints, not on-premises IoT devices.

notable_similarities: Identical Confluence login page HTML with the same hardcoded atlassian-token, build number (8703), and base-url placeholder across all devices and ports — strongly indicating a shared template or honeypot deployment rather than real Confluence instances.

Every device presents an implausibly broad and heterogeneous service portfolio (20–55+ ports) combining enterprise IT, networking, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT fingerprints simultaneously — characteristic of high-interaction honeypots or IoT emulation platforms.

HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: Predominantly AS58224 (TCI - Telecommunication Company of Iran / Iran Information Technology Company PJSC), with a few devices on smaller Iranian ISPs (AS43754 ASIATECH, AS42337 RESPINA, AS31549 RASANA, AS204650 ERTEBATATESTABLEAVARVAND). All devices are country_code: IR.
common_patterns.os: Where detected, Microsoft Windows Server 2012 R2 is the only identified OS. Most devices have no OS fingerprint.
common_patterns.software: Near-universal use of Microsoft IIS (predominantly version 10.0) and ASP.NET across all HTTP services. jQuery (versions 2.1.0, 2.1.4, 3.6.0) and Twitter Bootstrap appear frequently as frontend libraries. Swagger UI appears on one device.
common_patterns.hardware: DICOM-104 (medical imaging protocol) is present on the vast majority of devices, making it the single strongest hardware/protocol commonality. DVR_IP ports appear on a subset of devices. IKE-500 (VPN) appears on a few.
common_patterns.services: DICOM-104 is the near-universal service. HTTP on various non-standard ports is common. MDNS-5353 (mDNS/Bonjour) appears on many devices. MIKROTIK_BW-2000 appears on several, indicating MikroTik network equipment. VPN-related services (IKE-500, L2TP-1701, PPTP-1723) appear on a subset. MSSQL-1433 (SQL Server 15.0.2000) appears on at least two devices.
common_patterns.http_tags_and_favicons: The most dominant HTTP application fingerprint is 'Marco Pacs' — a PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) — appearing across many devices on various ports (80, 443, 6527, 6528, 1360, etc.). Other medical software titles include 'OHIF Viewer' (DICOM web viewer), 'MedPacs', 'PayvastERP', and Persian-language medical/laboratory portals (online lab results, radiology results, hospital reporting panels). Titles are predominantly in Persian (Farsi).
common_patterns.certificates: Multiple devices share wildcard certificate CN=*.marcopacs.net issued by Certum (Unizeto Technologies S.A. / Asseco Data Systems S.A., Poland), confirming a shared Marco PACS deployment. One device has CN=pacsoxin.com from the same Certum CA.
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS is largely absent. One device resolves to shatel.ir (an Iranian ISP).

distribution_characteristics.geographic: All 44 devices are located in Iran (IR). No cross-country distribution.
distribution_characteristics.organizational: Majority are under TCI (Telecommunication Company of Iran) and its subsidiary Iran Information Technology Company PJSC — the dominant national telecom. A minority are on smaller Iranian commercial ISPs (Asiatech, Respina, Shatel, Ertebat Sabet). This suggests these are customer-premise deployments (hospitals/clinics) connected via various Iranian ISPs, not a single data center.
distribution_characteristics.network_blocks: Devices span multiple /21 to /24 BGP prefixes, consistent with geographically distributed end-customer sites rather than a co-located deployment.

notable_similarities: DICOM-104 open port is the strongest clustering signal — present on nearly all devices, identifying them as medical imaging systems (PACS servers).
Marco PACS application (title 'Marco Pacs', wildcard cert *.marcopacs.net) is deployed across a large subset, indicating a single Iranian medical imaging software vendor's customer base.
Uniform Microsoft IIS 10.0 + ASP.NET stack across all HTTP-serving devices points to a standardized deployment template.
MDNS-5353 exposure on many devices suggests local-network service discovery is inadvertently exposed to the internet, a common misconfiguration in clinical environments.
MikroTik presence (MIKROTIK_BW-2000, RouterOS HTTP title) on several devices indicates MikroTik routers are used as the network gateway at these sites, with management interfaces exposed.
Persian-language web UIs (lab results, radiology, hospital HIS portals) confirm these are Iranian healthcare facility deployments.
Shared Certum CA (Polish CA) for *.marcopacs.net certificates across multiple IPs confirms a single vendor (Marco PACS) managing TLS certificates for its customer installations.
DVR_IP ports on a subset suggest co-located IP camera/DVR systems at the same facilities, broadening the attack surface.
report.cluster_summary: This cluster represents Iranian healthcare facility servers — primarily hospitals and diagnostic imaging centers — running the Marco PACS medical imaging platform (and related HIS/lab software) on a standardized Microsoft IIS/ASP.NET stack. The near-universal presence of open DICOM-104 ports, shared *.marcopacs.net wildcard certificates, and Persian-language medical web portals confirm these are deployments of a single Iranian medical software vendor across distributed clinical sites. Security concerns include exposed DICOM, mDNS, MikroTik management interfaces, DVR ports, and in some cases open MSSQL and SMB services directly on the internet.

common_patterns.os: Where detected, Microsoft Windows Server 2012 R2 is the only identified OS. Most devices have no OS fingerprint.
common_patterns.software: Near-universal use of Microsoft IIS (predominantly version 10.0) and ASP.NET across all HTTP services. jQuery (versions 2.1.0, 2.1.4, 3.6.0) and Twitter Bootstrap appear frequently as frontend libraries. Swagger UI appears on one device.
common_patterns.hardware: DICOM-104 (medical imaging protocol) is present on the vast majority of devices, making it the single strongest hardware/protocol commonality. DVR_IP ports appear on a subset of devices. IKE-500 (VPN) appears on a few.
common_patterns.services: DICOM-104 is the near-universal service. HTTP on various non-standard ports is common. MDNS-5353 (mDNS/Bonjour) appears on many devices. MIKROTIK_BW-2000 appears on several, indicating MikroTik network equipment. VPN-related services (IKE-500, L2TP-1701, PPTP-1723) appear on a subset. MSSQL-1433 (SQL Server 15.0.2000) appears on at least two devices.
common_patterns.http_tags_and_favicons: The most dominant HTTP application fingerprint is 'Marco Pacs' — a PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) — appearing across many devices on various ports (80, 443, 6527, 6528, 1360, etc.). Other medical software titles include 'OHIF Viewer' (DICOM web viewer), 'MedPacs', 'PayvastERP', and Persian-language medical/laboratory portals (online lab results, radiology results, hospital reporting panels). Titles are predominantly in Persian (Farsi).
common_patterns.certificates: Multiple devices share wildcard certificate CN=*.marcopacs.net issued by Certum (Unizeto Technologies S.A. / Asseco Data Systems S.A., Poland), confirming a shared Marco PACS deployment. One device has CN=pacsoxin.com from the same Certum CA.
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS is largely absent. One device resolves to shatel.ir (an Iranian ISP).

distribution_characteristics.geographic: All 44 devices are located in Iran (IR). No cross-country distribution.
distribution_characteristics.organizational: Majority are under TCI (Telecommunication Company of Iran) and its subsidiary Iran Information Technology Company PJSC — the dominant national telecom. A minority are on smaller Iranian commercial ISPs (Asiatech, Respina, Shatel, Ertebat Sabet). This suggests these are customer-premise deployments (hospitals/clinics) connected via various Iranian ISPs, not a single data center.
distribution_characteristics.network_blocks: Devices span multiple /21 to /24 BGP prefixes, consistent with geographically distributed end-customer sites rather than a co-located deployment.

notable_similarities: DICOM-104 open port is the strongest clustering signal — present on nearly all devices, identifying them as medical imaging systems (PACS servers).
Marco PACS application (title 'Marco Pacs', wildcard cert *.marcopacs.net) is deployed across a large subset, indicating a single Iranian medical imaging software vendor's customer base.
Uniform Microsoft IIS 10.0 + ASP.NET stack across all HTTP-serving devices points to a standardized deployment template.
MDNS-5353 exposure on many devices suggests local-network service discovery is inadvertently exposed to the internet, a common misconfiguration in clinical environments.
MikroTik presence (MIKROTIK_BW-2000, RouterOS HTTP title) on several devices indicates MikroTik routers are used as the network gateway at these sites, with management interfaces exposed.
Persian-language web UIs (lab results, radiology, hospital HIS portals) confirm these are Iranian healthcare facility deployments.
Shared Certum CA (Polish CA) for *.marcopacs.net certificates across multiple IPs confirms a single vendor (Marco PACS) managing TLS certificates for its customer installations.
DVR_IP ports on a subset suggest co-located IP camera/DVR systems at the same facilities, broadening the attack surface.
report.cluster_summary: This cluster represents Iranian healthcare facility servers — primarily hospitals and diagnostic imaging centers — running the Marco PACS medical imaging platform (and related HIS/lab software) on a standardized Microsoft IIS/ASP.NET stack. The near-universal presence of open DICOM-104 ports, shared *.marcopacs.net wildcard certificates, and Persian-language medical web portals confirm these are deployments of a single Iranian medical software vendor across distributed clinical sites. Security concerns include exposed DICOM, mDNS, MikroTik management interfaces, DVR ports, and in some cases open MSSQL and SMB services directly on the internet.

os_vendor: No OS vendor information available across all sampled devices
os_product: No OS product information available across all sampled devices

overall: 100% of sampled devices have empty OS fingerprint fields, suggesting

cert_subjects: Overwhelming majority are self-signed Ubiquiti Networks Inc. certificates with OU=Technical Support, CN=UBNT-<MAC_ADDRESS>, emailAddress=support@ubnt.com. One outlier (65.18.203.76) uses a Microhard Systems Inc. self-signed cert.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: All devices belong to Amazon AS16509 (AMAZON-02) or AS14618 (AMAZON-AES), hosted across multiple AWS regions (eu-west-2, af-south-1, us-east-1, us-west-2, ap-northeast-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1)
common_patterns.os: Predominantly Linux-based (Debian, Kamikaze/OpenWrt, RedHat); one Windows instance (158.252.85.105); OS versions largely unknown
common_patterns.software: Highly heterogeneous software stack per device — each IP exposes 40-60+ HTTP services simultaneously including: Fortinet (FortiGate, FortiSwitch, FortiManager), ASUS AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Atlassian Confluence, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, CyberPanel, ComfyUI, Ray Dashboard, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver, Palo Alto GlobalProtect, BeyondTrust Remote Support, WordPress, miniupnpd, aiohttp/Python
common_patterns.hardware: Recurring hardware fingerprints: Fortinet FortiSwitch, ASUS RT-AX68U, EasyIO 30P, Electroind Gaugetech, SonicWall SMA, Veeam Backup Server, Merit Lilin PDR-M800
common_patterns.service_distribution: Each device exposes an unusually large number of ports (40-60+), spanning HTTP on non-standard ports, MQTT (1883/8883), MQTT-TLS, DNS-53, REDIS-6379, MONGODB-27017, POSTGRES-5432/26257, SSH-22/2222, MDNS-5353, MSMQ-1801, SMB-110/445, IMAP-143, and numerous Unknown Protocol entries
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Recurring page titles across devices: FortiManager-VM64, FortiSwitch Login, FortiGate, ASUS Login/AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Mirth Connect Administrator, PaperCut Login, CrushFTP WebInterface, Confluence Login, ComfyUI, Ray Dashboard, ServiceNow, CyberPanel Login, Download Master, USG310, GlobalProtect Portal, SAP NetWeaver, EasyIO-30P Sedona
common_patterns.certificates: Extremely diverse and mismatched TLS certificates — subjects include IoT devices (August Lock, SmartThings, Honeywell Thermostat, Philips Hue, Dahua, AXIS, Reolink), ICS/SCADA systems (SIMATIC WinCC, DeltaV/Emerson, IEC61850-Server, BACnet-Controller, iFIX/GE, Yokogawa CENTUM), network gear (FortiGate, Palo Alto, SonicWall, Cisco ASA, Draytek, Aruba, Juniper), enterprise software (Kubernetes, Azure AD, SharePoint, Veeam, Dell iDRAC), and financial/healthcare entities. All use TLSv1.3
common_patterns.dns: All reverse DNS entries resolve to AWS EC2 compute hostnames (*.compute.amazonaws.com) across regions

distribution_characteristics.geographic: AWS EC2 instances spread globally: EU West (London), Africa South (Cape Town), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), AP Northeast (Tokyo x2, Osaka x2), Middle East (UAE)
distribution_characteristics.organizational: All WHOIS records point to Amazon Data Services subsidiaries (UK, South Africa, Northern Virginia, UAE, Osaka) or Amazon Technologies Inc. — no non-Amazon ASNs present in the sample
distribution_characteristics.port_density: Each device consistently exposes 40-60+ distinct services, far exceeding typical single-purpose device behavior, suggesting these are honeypots or scanning infrastructure rather than real production devices

notable_similarities: Every device presents multiple conflicting service identities simultaneously on different ports — e.g., the same IP serves FortiManager, ASUS AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Confluence, and ComfyUI concurrently, which is physically impossible for a single real device

TLS certificates are systematically mismatched: certificate subjects reference internal hostnames, IoT device MACs, ICS system names, and enterprise infrastructure that have no relationship to the AWS IP or each other, indicating synthetic/spoofed certificate data

The same set of ~15-20 application fingerprints (FortiSwitch, AiCloud, Ivanti, Mirth Connect, PaperCut, CyberPanel, ComfyUI, Ray Dashboard, Confluence, ServiceNow, EasyIO-30P) recurs across all 10 sampled IPs regardless of region, suggesting templated service simulation

MQTT (1883/8883), Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL appear across multiple devices alongside HTTP services, consistent with IoT honeypot infrastructure designed to attract diverse scanner/attacker profiles

Hardware fingerprints (FortiSwitch, ASUS RT-AX68U, EasyIO 30P, Gaugetech) repeat identically across geographically dispersed IPs, which would be statistically improbable for organic device deployments
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 consists of 3532 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally, each simulating a large number of heterogeneous IoT, OT, network, and enterprise services simultaneously on dozens of non-standard ports — a pattern strongly indicative of honeypot or deception infrastructure. The devices share a common fingerprint template featuring recurring application titles, hardware identifiers, and TLS certificate patterns that are internally inconsistent and mismatched to their AWS hosting context. The cluster is unified by its AWS-only hosting, extreme port/service density per IP, synthetic certificate diversity, and the systematic co-presence of IoT, ICS/SCADA, VPN, and enterprise application fingerprints that no single physical device could legitimately host.

The highly heterogeneous and mismatched service/certificate combinations, templated HTML responses, and globally distributed AWS infrastructure strongly indicate this cluster represents a large-scale honeypot or cyber deception network designed to attract and fingerprint threat actors. The uniform underlying OS (Debian/Linux on AWS EC2) and exclusive use of TLSv1.3 across all nodes confirm a common deployment framework beneath the diverse device personas.

common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: All devices belong to AS16509 (AMAZON-02) or AS14618 (AMAZON-AES), both operated by Amazon.com, Inc. — 100% AWS-hosted infrastructure.
common_patterns.whois: Devices span multiple Amazon regional data center network handles: AWS-BKK, AMAZO-ZFRA, AMAZON-CDG, AMAZON-CPT, AMAZON-KIX, AMAZON-DXB, AMAZON-CGK — all under Amazon organizational ownership.
common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.
common_patterns.hardware: HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U are the most frequently fingerprinted hardware across devices, often co-occurring on the same IP. Fortinet FortiSwitch hardware also recurs. These are likely honeypot or emulated device signatures.
common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. Mix of HTTP, Unknown Protocol (TLS-wrapped), DNS, MQTT, SMB, IPP, SSH, SSDP/UPnP, and PostgreSQL services. No device is limited to a single service role.
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Confluence login page HTML (identical atlassian-token 'e68dfa45d0ec9701eac9e51568b6020923c96741', build number 8703, base-url 'https://www.example.com') is replicated verbatim across all devices and ports. FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate login pages, GlobalProtect Portal, ASUS Login, CyberPanel, PaperCut, Ray Dashboard, Mirth Connect, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver pages also recur across multiple IPs.
common_patterns.certificates: TLS certificates are highly diverse and inconsistent per port — mixing legitimate CA-signed certs (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust, Amazon) with self-signed device certs (Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, Siemens, HP, MikroTik, Honeywell, ICS/SCADA vendors). Certificate subjects frequently reference ICS/OT systems (SCADA, PLC, IEC61850, DNP3, Honeywell Experion, Yokogawa CENTUM, Siemens SIMATIC WinCC), healthcare (EMR, DICOM, Epic, Allscripts, DirectTrust), and enterprise IT (Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Splunk, HashiCorp Vault).
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS consistently resolves to AWS EC2 regional hostnames (ap-southeast-7, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, af-south-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1, ap-southeast-3). Two devices (54.85.68.8, 18.216.147.127) have no reverse DNS.

distribution_characteristics.geographic: Global AWS footprint spanning at least 8 regions: AP Southeast (Bangkok), EU Central (Frankfurt), EU West (Paris), AF South (Cape Town), AP Northeast (Osaka), ME Central (UAE), AP Southeast (Jakarta), US East (Ohio/Virginia).
distribution_characteristics.organizational: All devices are AWS EC2 instances across Amazon's regional data center subsidiaries. No non-Amazon ASNs present. The cluster represents a globally distributed set of AWS-hosted endpoints, not on-premises IoT devices.

notable_similarities: Identical Confluence login page HTML with the same hardcoded atlassian-token, build number (8703), and base-url placeholder across all devices and ports — strongly indicating a shared template or honeypot deployment rather than real Confluence instances.

Every device presents an implausibly broad and heterogeneous service portfolio (20–55+ ports) combining enterprise IT, networking, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT fingerprints simultaneously — characteristic of high-interaction honeypots or IoT emulation platforms.

HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 consists of 3532 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally, each simulating a large number of heterogeneous IoT, OT, network, and enterprise services simultaneously on dozens of non-standard ports — a pattern strongly indicative of honeypot or deception infrastructure. The devices share a common fingerprint template featuring recurring application titles, hardware identifiers, and TLS certificate patterns that are internally inconsistent and mismatched to their AWS hosting context. The cluster is unified by its AWS-only hosting, extreme port/service density per IP, synthetic certificate diversity, and the systematic co-presence of IoT, ICS/SCADA, VPN, and enterprise application fingerprints that no single physical device could legitimately host.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.os: Predominantly Linux-based (Debian, Kamikaze/OpenWrt, RedHat); one Windows instance (158.252.85.105); OS versions largely unknown
common_patterns.software: Highly heterogeneous software stack per device — each IP exposes 40-60+ HTTP services simultaneously including: Fortinet (FortiGate, FortiSwitch, FortiManager), ASUS AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Atlassian Confluence, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, CyberPanel, ComfyUI, Ray Dashboard, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver, Palo Alto GlobalProtect, BeyondTrust Remote Support, WordPress, miniupnpd, aiohttp/Python
common_patterns.hardware: Recurring hardware fingerprints: Fortinet FortiSwitch, ASUS RT-AX68U, EasyIO 30P, Electroind Gaugetech, SonicWall SMA, Veeam Backup Server, Merit Lilin PDR-M800
common_patterns.service_distribution: Each device exposes an unusually large number of ports (40-60+), spanning HTTP on non-standard ports, MQTT (1883/8883), MQTT-TLS, DNS-53, REDIS-6379, MONGODB-27017, POSTGRES-5432/26257, SSH-22/2222, MDNS-5353, MSMQ-1801, SMB-110/445, IMAP-143, and numerous Unknown Protocol entries
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Recurring page titles across devices: FortiManager-VM64, FortiSwitch Login, FortiGate, ASUS Login/AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Mirth Connect Administrator, PaperCut Login, CrushFTP WebInterface, Confluence Login, ComfyUI, Ray Dashboard, ServiceNow, CyberPanel Login, Download Master, USG310, GlobalProtect Portal, SAP NetWeaver, EasyIO-30P Sedona
common_patterns.certificates: Extremely diverse and mismatched TLS certificates — subjects include IoT devices (August Lock, SmartThings, Honeywell Thermostat, Philips Hue, Dahua, AXIS, Reolink), ICS/SCADA systems (SIMATIC WinCC, DeltaV/Emerson, IEC61850-Server, BACnet-Controller, iFIX/GE, Yokogawa CENTUM), network gear (FortiGate, Palo Alto, SonicWall, Cisco ASA, Draytek, Aruba, Juniper), enterprise software (Kubernetes, Azure AD, SharePoint, Veeam, Dell iDRAC), and financial/healthcare entities. All use TLSv1.3
common_patterns.dns: All reverse DNS entries resolve to AWS EC2 compute hostnames (*.compute.amazonaws.com) across regions

distribution_characteristics.geographic: AWS EC2 instances spread globally: EU West (London), Africa South (Cape Town), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), AP Northeast (Tokyo x2, Osaka x2), Middle East (UAE)
distribution_characteristics.organizational: All WHOIS records point to Amazon Data Services subsidiaries (UK, South Africa, Northern Virginia, UAE, Osaka) or Amazon Technologies Inc. — no non-Amazon ASNs present in the sample
distribution_characteristics.port_density: Each device consistently exposes 40-60+ distinct services, far exceeding typical single-purpose device behavior, suggesting these are honeypots or scanning infrastructure rather than real production devices

notable_similarities: Every device presents multiple conflicting service identities simultaneously on different ports — e.g., the same IP serves FortiManager, ASUS AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Confluence, and ComfyUI concurrently, which is physically impossible for a single real device

TLS certificates are systematically mismatched: certificate subjects reference internal hostnames, IoT device MACs, ICS system names, and enterprise infrastructure that have no relationship to the AWS IP or each other, indicating synthetic/spoofed certificate data

The same set of ~15-20 application fingerprints (FortiSwitch, AiCloud, Ivanti, Mirth Connect, PaperCut, CyberPanel, ComfyUI, Ray Dashboard, Confluence, ServiceNow, EasyIO-30P) recurs across all 10 sampled IPs regardless of region, suggesting templated service simulation

MQTT (1883/8883), Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL appear across multiple devices alongside HTTP services, consistent with IoT honeypot infrastructure designed to attract diverse scanner/attacker profiles

Hardware fingerprints (FortiSwitch, ASUS RT-AX68U, EasyIO 30P, Gaugetech) repeat identically across geographically dispersed IPs, which would be statistically improbable for organic device deployments
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 consists of 3532 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally, each simulating a large number of heterogeneous IoT, OT, network, and enterprise services simultaneously on dozens of non-standard ports — a pattern strongly indicative of honeypot or deception infrastructure. The devices share a common fingerprint template featuring recurring application titles, hardware identifiers, and TLS certificate patterns that are internally inconsistent and mismatched to their AWS hosting context. The cluster is unified by its AWS-only hosting, extreme port/service density per IP, synthetic certificate diversity, and the systematic co-presence of IoT, ICS/SCADA, VPN, and enterprise application fingerprints that no single physical device could legitimately host.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: All devices belong to AS16509 (AMAZON-02) or AS14618 (AMAZON-AES), both operated by Amazon.com, Inc. — 100% AWS-hosted infrastructure.
common_patterns.whois: Devices span multiple Amazon regional data center network handles: AWS-BKK, AMAZO-ZFRA, AMAZON-CDG, AMAZON-CPT, AMAZON-KIX, AMAZON-DXB, AMAZON-CGK — all under Amazon organizational ownership.
common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.
common_patterns.hardware: HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U are the most frequently fingerprinted hardware across devices, often co-occurring on the same IP. Fortinet FortiSwitch hardware also recurs. These are likely honeypot or emulated device signatures.
common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. Mix of HTTP, Unknown Protocol (TLS-wrapped), DNS, MQTT, SMB, IPP, SSH, SSDP/UPnP, and PostgreSQL services. No device is limited to a single service role.
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Confluence login page HTML (identical atlassian-token 'e68dfa45d0ec9701eac9e51568b6020923c96741', build number 8703, base-url 'https://www.example.com') is replicated verbatim across all devices and ports. FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate login pages, GlobalProtect Portal, ASUS Login, CyberPanel, PaperCut, Ray Dashboard, Mirth Connect, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver pages also recur across multiple IPs.
common_patterns.certificates: TLS certificates are highly diverse and inconsistent per port — mixing legitimate CA-signed certs (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust, Amazon) with self-signed device certs (Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, Siemens, HP, MikroTik, Honeywell, ICS/SCADA vendors). Certificate subjects frequently reference ICS/OT systems (SCADA, PLC, IEC61850, DNP3, Honeywell Experion, Yokogawa CENTUM, Siemens SIMATIC WinCC), healthcare (EMR, DICOM, Epic, Allscripts, DirectTrust), and enterprise IT (Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Splunk, HashiCorp Vault).
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS consistently resolves to AWS EC2 regional hostnames (ap-southeast-7, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, af-south-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1, ap-southeast-3). Two devices (54.85.68.8, 18.216.147.127) have no reverse DNS.

distribution_characteristics.geographic: Global AWS footprint spanning at least 8 regions: AP Southeast (Bangkok), EU Central (Frankfurt), EU West (Paris), AF South (Cape Town), AP Northeast (Osaka), ME Central (UAE), AP Southeast (Jakarta), US East (Ohio/Virginia).
distribution_characteristics.organizational: All devices are AWS EC2 instances across Amazon's regional data center subsidiaries. No non-Amazon ASNs present. The cluster represents a globally distributed set of AWS-hosted endpoints, not on-premises IoT devices.

notable_similarities: Identical Confluence login page HTML with the same hardcoded atlassian-token, build number (8703), and base-url placeholder across all devices and ports — strongly indicating a shared template or honeypot deployment rather than real Confluence instances.

Every device presents an implausibly broad and heterogeneous service portfolio (20–55+ ports) combining enterprise IT, networking, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT fingerprints simultaneously — characteristic of high-interaction honeypots or IoT emulation platforms.

HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.
common_patterns.hardware: HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U are the most frequently fingerprinted hardware across devices, often co-occurring on the same IP. Fortinet FortiSwitch hardware also recurs. These are likely honeypot or emulated device signatures.
common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. Mix of HTTP, Unknown Protocol (TLS-wrapped), DNS, MQTT, SMB, IPP, SSH, SSDP/UPnP, and PostgreSQL services. No device is limited to a single service role.
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Confluence login page HTML (identical atlassian-token 'e68dfa45d0ec9701eac9e51568b6020923c96741', build number 8703, base-url 'https://www.example.com') is replicated verbatim across all devices and ports. FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate login pages, GlobalProtect Portal, ASUS Login, CyberPanel, PaperCut, Ray Dashboard, Mirth Connect, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver pages also recur across multiple IPs.
common_patterns.certificates: TLS certificates are highly diverse and inconsistent per port — mixing legitimate CA-signed certs (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust, Amazon) with self-signed device certs (Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, Siemens, HP, MikroTik, Honeywell, ICS/SCADA vendors). Certificate subjects frequently reference ICS/OT systems (SCADA, PLC, IEC61850, DNP3, Honeywell Experion, Yokogawa CENTUM, Siemens SIMATIC WinCC), healthcare (EMR, DICOM, Epic, Allscripts, DirectTrust), and enterprise IT (Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Splunk, HashiCorp Vault).
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS consistently resolves to AWS EC2 regional hostnames (ap-southeast-7, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, af-south-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1, ap-southeast-3). Two devices (54.85.68.8, 18.216.147.127) have no reverse DNS.

distribution_characteristics.geographic: Global AWS footprint spanning at least 8 regions: AP Southeast (Bangkok), EU Central (Frankfurt), EU West (Paris), AF South (Cape Town), AP Northeast (Osaka), ME Central (UAE), AP Southeast (Jakarta), US East (Ohio/Virginia).
distribution_characteristics.organizational: All devices are AWS EC2 instances across Amazon's regional data center subsidiaries. No non-Amazon ASNs present. The cluster represents a globally distributed set of AWS-hosted endpoints, not on-premises IoT devices.

notable_similarities: Identical Confluence login page HTML with the same hardcoded atlassian-token, build number (8703), and base-url placeholder across all devices and ports — strongly indicating a shared template or honeypot deployment rather than real Confluence instances.

Every device presents an implausibly broad and heterogeneous service portfolio (20–55+ ports) combining enterprise IT, networking, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT fingerprints simultaneously — characteristic of high-interaction honeypots or IoT emulation platforms.

HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

distribution_characteristics.port_density: Each device consistently exposes 40-60+ distinct services, far exceeding typical single-purpose device behavior, suggesting these are honeypots or scanning infrastructure rather than real production devices

notable_similarities: Every device presents multiple conflicting service identities simultaneously on different ports — e.g., the same IP serves FortiManager, ASUS AiCloud, Ivanti Connect Secure, Confluence, and ComfyUI concurrently, which is physically impossible for a single real device

TLS certificates are systematically mismatched: certificate subjects reference internal hostnames, IoT device MACs, ICS system names, and enterprise infrastructure that have no relationship to the AWS IP or each other, indicating synthetic/spoofed certificate data

The same set of ~15-20 application fingerprints (FortiSwitch, AiCloud, Ivanti, Mirth Connect, PaperCut, CyberPanel, ComfyUI, Ray Dashboard, Confluence, ServiceNow, EasyIO-30P) recurs across all 10 sampled IPs regardless of region, suggesting templated service simulation

MQTT (1883/8883), Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL appear across multiple devices alongside HTTP services, consistent with IoT honeypot infrastructure designed to attract diverse scanner/attacker profiles

Hardware fingerprints (FortiSwitch, ASUS RT-AX68U, EasyIO 30P, Gaugetech) repeat identically across geographically dispersed IPs, which would be statistically improbable for organic device deployments
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 consists of 3532 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally, each simulating a large number of heterogeneous IoT, OT, network, and enterprise services simultaneously on dozens of non-standard ports — a pattern strongly indicative of honeypot or deception infrastructure. The devices share a common fingerprint template featuring recurring application titles, hardware identifiers, and TLS certificate patterns that are internally inconsistent and mismatched to their AWS hosting context. The cluster is unified by its AWS-only hosting, extreme port/service density per IP, synthetic certificate diversity, and the systematic co-presence of IoT, ICS/SCADA, VPN, and enterprise application fingerprints that no single physical device could legitimately host.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: Predominantly AS58224 (TCI - Telecommunication Company of Iran / Iran Information Technology Company PJSC), with a few devices on smaller Iranian ISPs (AS43754 ASIATECH, AS42337 RESPINA, AS31549 RASANA, AS204650 ERTEBATATESTABLEAVARVAND). All devices are country_code: IR.
common_patterns.os: Where detected, Microsoft Windows Server 2012 R2 is the only identified OS. Most devices have no OS fingerprint.
common_patterns.software: Near-universal use of Microsoft IIS (predominantly version 10.0) and ASP.NET across all HTTP services. jQuery (versions 2.1.0, 2.1.4, 3.6.0) and Twitter Bootstrap appear frequently as frontend libraries. Swagger UI appears on one device.
common_patterns.hardware: DICOM-104 (medical imaging protocol) is present on the vast majority of devices, making it the single strongest hardware/protocol commonality. DVR_IP ports appear on a subset of devices. IKE-500 (VPN) appears on a few.
common_patterns.services: DICOM-104 is the near-universal service. HTTP on various non-standard ports is common. MDNS-5353 (mDNS/Bonjour) appears on many devices. MIKROTIK_BW-2000 appears on several, indicating MikroTik network equipment. VPN-related services (IKE-500, L2TP-1701, PPTP-1723) appear on a subset. MSSQL-1433 (SQL Server 15.0.2000) appears on at least two devices.
common_patterns.http_tags_and_favicons: The most dominant HTTP application fingerprint is 'Marco Pacs' — a PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) — appearing across many devices on various ports (80, 443, 6527, 6528, 1360, etc.). Other medical software titles include 'OHIF Viewer' (DICOM web viewer), 'MedPacs', 'PayvastERP', and Persian-language medical/laboratory portals (online lab results, radiology results, hospital reporting panels). Titles are predominantly in Persian (Farsi).
common_patterns.certificates: Multiple devices share wildcard certificate CN=*.marcopacs.net issued by Certum (Unizeto Technologies S.A. / Asseco Data Systems S.A., Poland), confirming a shared Marco PACS deployment. One device has CN=pacsoxin.com from the same Certum CA.
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS is largely absent. One device resolves to shatel.ir (an Iranian ISP).

distribution_characteristics.geographic: All 44 devices are located in Iran (IR). No cross-country distribution.
distribution_characteristics.organizational: Majority are under TCI (Telecommunication Company of Iran) and its subsidiary Iran Information Technology Company PJSC — the dominant national telecom. A minority are on smaller Iranian commercial ISPs (Asiatech, Respina, Shatel, Ertebat Sabet). This suggests these are customer-premise deployments (hospitals/clinics) connected via various Iranian ISPs, not a single data center.
distribution_characteristics.network_blocks: Devices span multiple /21 to /24 BGP prefixes, consistent with geographically distributed end-customer sites rather than a co-located deployment.

notable_similarities: DICOM-104 open port is the strongest clustering signal — present on nearly all devices, identifying them as medical imaging systems (PACS servers).
Marco PACS application (title 'Marco Pacs', wildcard cert *.marcopacs.net) is deployed across a large subset, indicating a single Iranian medical imaging software vendor's customer base.
Uniform Microsoft IIS 10.0 + ASP.NET stack across all HTTP-serving devices points to a standardized deployment template.
MDNS-5353 exposure on many devices suggests local-network service discovery is inadvertently exposed to the internet, a common misconfiguration in clinical environments.
MikroTik presence (MIKROTIK_BW-2000, RouterOS HTTP title) on several devices indicates MikroTik routers are used as the network gateway at these sites, with management interfaces exposed.
Persian-language web UIs (lab results, radiology, hospital HIS portals) confirm these are Iranian healthcare facility deployments.
Shared Certum CA (Polish CA) for *.marcopacs.net certificates across multiple IPs confirms a single vendor (Marco PACS) managing TLS certificates for its customer installations.
DVR_IP ports on a subset suggest co-located IP camera/DVR systems at the same facilities, broadening the attack surface.
report.cluster_summary: This cluster represents Iranian healthcare facility servers — primarily hospitals and diagnostic imaging centers — running the Marco PACS medical imaging platform (and related HIS/lab software) on a standardized Microsoft IIS/ASP.NET stack. The near-universal presence of open DICOM-104 ports, shared *.marcopacs.net wildcard certificates, and Persian-language medical web portals confirm these are deployments of a single Iranian medical software vendor across distributed clinical sites. Security concerns include exposed DICOM, mDNS, MikroTik management interfaces, DVR ports, and in some cases open MSSQL and SMB services directly on the internet.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.autonomous_system: All devices belong to AS16509 (AMAZON-02) or AS14618 (AMAZON-AES), both operated by Amazon.com, Inc. — 100% AWS-hosted infrastructure.
common_patterns.whois: Devices span multiple Amazon regional data center network handles: AWS-BKK, AMAZO-ZFRA, AMAZON-CDG, AMAZON-CPT, AMAZON-KIX, AMAZON-DXB, AMAZON-CGK — all under Amazon organizational ownership.
common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.
common_patterns.hardware: HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U are the most frequently fingerprinted hardware across devices, often co-occurring on the same IP. Fortinet FortiSwitch hardware also recurs. These are likely honeypot or emulated device signatures.
common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. Mix of HTTP, Unknown Protocol (TLS-wrapped), DNS, MQTT, SMB, IPP, SSH, SSDP/UPnP, and PostgreSQL services. No device is limited to a single service role.
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Confluence login page HTML (identical atlassian-token 'e68dfa45d0ec9701eac9e51568b6020923c96741', build number 8703, base-url 'https://www.example.com') is replicated verbatim across all devices and ports. FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate login pages, GlobalProtect Portal, ASUS Login, CyberPanel, PaperCut, Ray Dashboard, Mirth Connect, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver pages also recur across multiple IPs.
common_patterns.certificates: TLS certificates are highly diverse and inconsistent per port — mixing legitimate CA-signed certs (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust, Amazon) with self-signed device certs (Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, Siemens, HP, MikroTik, Honeywell, ICS/SCADA vendors). Certificate subjects frequently reference ICS/OT systems (SCADA, PLC, IEC61850, DNP3, Honeywell Experion, Yokogawa CENTUM, Siemens SIMATIC WinCC), healthcare (EMR, DICOM, Epic, Allscripts, DirectTrust), and enterprise IT (Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Splunk, HashiCorp Vault).
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS consistently resolves to AWS EC2 regional hostnames (ap-southeast-7, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, af-south-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1, ap-southeast-3). Two devices (54.85.68.8, 18.216.147.127) have no reverse DNS.

distribution_characteristics.geographic: Global AWS footprint spanning at least 8 regions: AP Southeast (Bangkok), EU Central (Frankfurt), EU West (Paris), AF South (Cape Town), AP Northeast (Osaka), ME Central (UAE), AP Southeast (Jakarta), US East (Ohio/Virginia).
distribution_characteristics.organizational: All devices are AWS EC2 instances across Amazon's regional data center subsidiaries. No non-Amazon ASNs present. The cluster represents a globally distributed set of AWS-hosted endpoints, not on-premises IoT devices.

notable_similarities: Identical Confluence login page HTML with the same hardcoded atlassian-token, build number (8703), and base-url placeholder across all devices and ports — strongly indicating a shared template or honeypot deployment rather than real Confluence instances.

Every device presents an implausibly broad and heterogeneous service portfolio (20–55+ ports) combining enterprise IT, networking, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT fingerprints simultaneously — characteristic of high-interaction honeypots or IoT emulation platforms.

HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 consists of 3532 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally, each simulating a large number of heterogeneous IoT, OT, network, and enterprise services simultaneously on dozens of non-standard ports — a pattern strongly indicative of honeypot or deception infrastructure. The devices share a common fingerprint template featuring recurring application titles, hardware identifiers, and TLS certificate patterns that are internally inconsistent and mismatched to their AWS hosting context. The cluster is unified by its AWS-only hosting, extreme port/service density per IP, synthetic certificate diversity, and the systematic co-presence of IoT, ICS/SCADA, VPN, and enterprise application fingerprints that no single physical device could legitimately host.

HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.

common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U hardware fingerprints co-occur on the same IPs alongside enterprise software like Confluence and Fortinet — a combination that would not exist on real devices, reinforcing the honeypot/emulation hypothesis.

TLS certificates reference an unusually diverse set of organizations (ICS vendors, healthcare systems, financial institutions, cloud providers) on a single IP, consistent with certificate spoofing used in deception infrastructure.
All IPs resolve to AWS EC2 instances across multiple global regions, suggesting coordinated deployment of a distributed sensor or honeypot network rather than organically discovered IoT devices.
report.cluster_summary: Cluster 2 consists of 5,553 AWS EC2 instances distributed globally across 8+ AWS regions, each presenting an artificially broad and heterogeneous set of emulated services spanning enterprise IT, networking equipment, ICS/OT, healthcare, and consumer IoT. The defining signature is the verbatim replication of a Confluence login page (identical token, build number, and placeholder URL) across all devices and ports, combined with implausible hardware/software co-occurrences and spoofed TLS certificates from dozens of unrelated vendors. This cluster almost certainly represents a coordinated honeypot or IoT emulation/deception infrastructure rather than real IoT devices.

report.cluster_summary: Cluster 3 represents 69,104 Synology NAS devices (DiskStation/NAS/NVR) running DSM, deployed primarily in residential and small-office networks across global consumer ISPs. The defining fingerprint is the Synology DSM web interface on ports 5000/5001 with characteristic HTML metadata, webman favicon paths, nginx reverse proxy, and Synology-issued self-signed TLS certificates. A significant subset of devices also run home automation stacks (Home Assistant, ioBroker, MQTT, Grafana), indicating these are multi-purpose home server hubs rather than pure storage appliances.

common_patterns.os: Highly heterogeneous and often misidentified OS fingerprints: HP OfficeJet/Photosmart/Designjet/JetDirect printers, Canonical Linux, Debian Linux — suggesting OS fingerprinting is unreliable or deliberately obfuscated on these hosts.
common_patterns.software: Atlassian Confluence Server is the single most dominant application, appearing across virtually all devices on varied non-standard ports (101, 832, 1682, 1701, 4841, 6001, 8703 build number consistent). Other recurring software: Fortinet FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate, Palo Alto GlobalProtect/PAN-OS, HP JetDirect, Boa HTTP server, Eclipse Jetty, Apache HTTP Server, CrushFTP, CyberPanel, PaperCut MF, Mirth Connect, SAP NetWeaver, Ray Dashboard (aiohttp/Python), ServiceNow, ASUS router interfaces.
common_patterns.hardware: HP JetDirect and ASUS RT-AX68U are the most frequently fingerprinted hardware across devices, often co-occurring on the same IP. Fortinet FortiSwitch hardware also recurs. These are likely honeypot or emulated device signatures.
common_patterns.service_distribution: Extremely wide port ranges per device — each IP exposes 20–55+ services simultaneously across both standard and non-standard ports. Mix of HTTP, Unknown Protocol (TLS-wrapped), DNS, MQTT, SMB, IPP, SSH, SSDP/UPnP, and PostgreSQL services. No device is limited to a single service role.
common_patterns.http_tags_favicons: Confluence login page HTML (identical atlassian-token 'e68dfa45d0ec9701eac9e51568b6020923c96741', build number 8703, base-url 'https://www.example.com') is replicated verbatim across all devices and ports. FortiSwitch/FortiManager/FortiGate login pages, GlobalProtect Portal, ASUS Login, CyberPanel, PaperCut, Ray Dashboard, Mirth Connect, ServiceNow, SAP NetWeaver pages also recur across multiple IPs.
common_patterns.certificates: TLS certificates are highly diverse and inconsistent per port — mixing legitimate CA-signed certs (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust, Amazon) with self-signed device certs (Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, Siemens, HP, MikroTik, Honeywell, ICS/SCADA vendors). Certificate subjects frequently reference ICS/OT systems (SCADA, PLC, IEC61850, DNP3, Honeywell Experion, Yokogawa CENTUM, Siemens SIMATIC WinCC), healthcare (EMR, DICOM, Epic, Allscripts, DirectTrust), and enterprise IT (Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Splunk, HashiCorp Vault).
common_patterns.dns: Reverse DNS consistently resolves to AWS EC2 regional hostnames (ap-southeast-7, eu-central-1, eu-west-3, af-south-1, ap-northeast-3, me-central-1, ap-southeast-3). Two devices (54.85.68.8, 18.216.147.127) have no reverse DNS.
